summary: Weekly POC sync reviewing INT8 vs FP8 quantization experiment results. Redwood presented perf deltas (latency and throughput) and quality impact assessments across the customer's prompt set. INT8 yields significant cost and throughput improvements with minimal quality regression on most prompts; FP8 shows slightly better quality in generative edge cases but requires more infra tuning. Agreed next steps: share full perf/quality artifacts, customer to provide gold set for deeper evaluation, schedule infra deep-dive.
transcript:
Header: 2025-08-26 15:00 PDT | Duration: 45m | Recording: yes
Attendees: Alex Carter (Redwood AE); Priya Nair (Redwood SE); Michael Huang (NimbleAI - Eng Mgr); Jasmine Lee (NimbleAI - ML Eng); Sara Patel (NimbleAI - Platform); Tom Rivera (NimbleAI - Data Sci)

[00:00:00] Alex (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we've got 45 minutes, quick agenda: results review, quality impacts, perf deltas, and next steps. Priya will run through the numbers.

[00:00:18] Priya (Redwood SE): Great, hi all. Quick note — some of the model names in our report got munged by the exporter so apologies if you see odd tokens, but the core is the INT8 vs FP8 comparison on the 13B family you gave us.

[00:00:35] Michael (Customer): Yep that sounds right. We're mostly focused on the 13B baseline, intent is to see if we can move to INT8 for cost reasons without losing user-facing quality.

[00:00:44] Jasmine (Customer): Also we want to verify edge-case safety — hallucination on long-context chats was a big concern last week.

[00:00:51] Priya: Totally. So top-line: INT8 gave us about 1.6-1.9x throughput uplift depending on batch config, and p99 latency dropped ~20-30% on average. Cost per token dropped ~35% vs FP16 baseline. FP8 showed intermediate perf — usually slightly slower than INT8 in our setup but with smaller quality delta on some generative prompts.

[00:01:20] Tom (Customer): When you say p99 dropped 20-30%, what's the absolute? Our target is under 400ms p99 for sync char generation.

[00:01:28] Priya: Good call. On your baseline 13B with your sequence distribution, p99 for FP16 was ~520ms. INT8 brought that to ~390-420ms depending on batching and KV cache hits; FP8 was around 420-440ms. So INT8 gets you into the ballpark but it's sensitive to KV cache warmup and prefix lengths.

[00:01:50] Sara (Platform): The KV cache sensitivity — is that something we can tune in the runtime or is it model-architecture dependent?

[00:01:58] Priya: Mostly runtime knobs — caching TTL, prefix caching heuristics, and batching window size. The runtime's continuous batching plus prefix caching avoids recomputing long prefixes, but quantization can amplify small FP errors which sometimes shows up after cache eviction.

[00:02:14] Alex: There's also an option to pin certain hot routes to FP16 while using INT8 for everything else — hybrid routing. That gives you predictable latency for the critical path.

[00:02:26] Michael: Interesting. How big was the quality regression with INT8 on your eval? We measured by exact-match and some automatic metrics but also a small human eval last week.

[00:02:36] Priya: For automatic metrics across your sample set — BLEU-ish style matching and task-oriented success — INT8 had a median drop of about 1.8% absolute. In human evals, overall preference for outputs between FP16 and INT8 was statistically indistinguishable for ~78% of prompts. The remaining cases were edge generative prompts where INT8 had slightly shorter or less detailed completions.

[00:02:58] Jasmine: The edge cases are the ones we care about — long multi-turn, instruction-following where small detail loss is visible. Did you try FP8 on those specifically?

[00:03:07] Priya: We did. FP8 reduced the detailed-completion drop; on the problematic prompt subset FP8 matched FP16 in about 85% of cases, whereas INT8 was about 70%. But FP8 added infra complexity — it's less widely supported in our runtime optimizations and required a couple of extra kernel paths.

[00:03:25] Tom: Extra complexity meaning more tuning and potentially less stable p99?

[00:03:30] Priya: Correct — we had to adjust kernel fallbacks and tweak the quantization scale parameters; in our tests FP8's p99 ended up slightly higher than INT8 but still below baseline FP16 in some configs. In others, it was comparable. So it's a tradeoff: quality vs operational surface area.

[00:03:49] Michael: Does FP8 require specific hardware or driver versions?

[00:03:53] Priya: It depends. On newer driver stacks and some GPUs it's fine, but on older infra you'd need specific libs / updated kernels. We'll include a compatibility matrix in the perf packet.

[00:04:05] Alex: Quick note on cost: we model both token-unit pricing and reserved capacity. If you move to INT8 on Dedicated, your unit cost effectively drops further because you get more throughput per GPU; we can share a modeled cost table.

[00:04:18] Michael: Please do — that'll help the finance folks.

[00:04:22] Sara: Any observed regression on safety checks — e.g., moderation classifier downstream? We can't have quantization amplifying hallucinations.

[00:04:30] Priya: We ran the moderation pipeline on outputs; overall the moderation recall/precision didn't materially change for INT8 on the sampled set. That said, in a handful of generative hallucinations, post-filter flags changed because of subtle tokenization differences; we'll highlight those exact examples.

[00:04:50] Jasmine: Would you recommend doing a mixed approach in production — INT8 for standard responses and FP16/FP8 for high-sensitivity routes?

[00:04:58] Priya: Yes, hybrid routing is our recommended approach when you need both cost savings and high fidelity in selected cases. Redwood's routing rules can pin model variants per route.

[00:05:08] Tom: On the benchmarks, did you measure memory footprints? We're constrained on GPU memory.

[00:05:13] Priya: INT8 lowers memory usage significantly — roughly 40% reduction in the model tensor footprint, which allowed us to increase effective batch sizes. FP8 had similar memory wins but needed additional workspace in some kernels.

[00:05:25] Michael: Any unexpected failure modes during the POC?

[00:05:28] Priya: One issue: during a stress test with long prefixes and forced cache evictions, we saw a small set of runs where token repetition probability changed slightly. We traced it to quantization scale drift on layernorm in a couple of layers; a short fix was to apply per-channel calibrations which reduced the effect. We'll include the patch and suggested calibration CLI args.

[00:05:50] Alex: We'll put those calibrations into the sample scripts we share.

[00:05:54] Sara: Sounds good. On the infra side, we need the perf traces to validate our autoscaler decisions. Can you share p50/p90/p99 timelines and the raw traces?

[00:06:03] Priya: Yes, we'll export the traces — per-request latencies, batch sizes, and cache-hit tags. Expect a CSV + basic plots.

[00:06:11] Jasmine: For the human eval, can you also share the sampled prompts where INT8 diverged so we can re-run internal checks?

[00:06:16] Priya: Absolutely. We'll annotate them with severity tags.

[00:06:20] Michael: If we move to a pilot on Dedicated, how long to get an environment with INT8 tuned?

[00:06:26] Alex: For Dedicated reserved capacity we can stand up an environment in a few days; tuning/validation to production-ready quality usually takes 1-2 weeks depending on how many routes you want pinned. The pilot agreement can be a 30-60 day pilot.

[00:06:40] Michael: Ok that's workable. Any security/compliance impacts from quantization?

[00:06:45] Priya: No direct compliance impact; the model weights are the same semantics. If you're running in Private (VPC/on-prem) there are no added data-plane exposures from quantization. We'll still provide signed attestations and the usual SOC2 artifacts.

[00:06:58] Sara: Good. Please include the KMS key integration notes in the packet as well.

[00:07:02] Priya: Will do.

[00:07:05] Alex: Alright let's walk through a couple of example screenshots from the perf packet — Priya?

[00:07:10] Priya: (screen-share noise) First chart: throughput by batching window — INT8 gets best throughput at slightly larger windows, but your latency constraint pushes the sweet spot smaller. Second: quality delta heatmap per prompt bucket — most buckets are green (under 2% delta) but there are a couple red buckets: multi-turn role-play and long code-gen like prompts.

[00:07:37] Tom: For code-gen we definitely need fidelity. If INT8 chops off details there, maybe we route code-gen to FP8 or FP16.

[00:07:45] Priya: Exactly. We can set route mapping to ensure code-gen model variants use higher precision.

[00:07:50] Michael: On next steps, I want the perf packet and the exact examples we discussed. Also, let's get a date for the infra deep-dive.

[00:07:57] Alex: We'll aim to get the artifact packet by Friday 2025-08-29. Deep-dive proposed 2025-09-04, we'll send a calendar invite.

[00:08:05] Jasmine: One operational question — do you support rolling quantization switches? Like A/B test users on FP16 vs INT8?

[00:08:12] Priya: Yes, Redwood supports canary and A/B rollouts by route/model. You can route X% of traffic to INT8 variant and monitor quality and error rates, then increase.

[00:08:22] Michael: Great. Any known incompatibilities with our on-prem GPU fleet? We're running a mix of A100s and a few older cards.

[00:08:30] Priya: Older cards may not support some FP8 kernels; INT8 is generally supported but performance characteristics differ. We'll include the compatibility matrix and recommended driver versions.

[00:08:40] Alex: Any final questions?

[00:08:43] Sara: Nothing else from infra.

[00:08:45] Tom: All good. I'll dig into the perf plots once shared.

[00:08:48] Jasmine: Thanks — excited to see the full set.

[00:08:51] Alex: Awesome — recap of action items: Priya share perf traces and annotated prompt diffs by 8/29; Alex share pricing/pilot doc by 8/28; customer sends 1k gold prompts by 9/2; schedule deep-dive for 9/4.

[00:09:08] Michael: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.

[00:09:12] Alex: Thanks, we'll follow up in email with links. Bye.

(Transcript ends — rest of meeting was off-record follow-up coordination)
